query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A hybrid prediction approach that integrates ab initio calculations of defect and oxygen impurity scattering with machine-learning calibration to experimental conductivity data will significantly reduce the prediction error of electrical conductivity for bulk, polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr (with ~1 wt.% oxygen) compared to conventional models based on perfect crystals.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr in a polycrystalline form, containing intrinsic defects and ~1 wt.% oxygen impurities.
generation.intervention: Develop and implement a computational model that couples ab initio defect scattering calculations (explicitly including oxygen impurity effects) with machine-learning submodels that are independently trained for the low (0–200 K) and high (300–1200 K) temperature regimes.
generation.conditions: Experiments and predictions conducted on bulk, polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr samples with ~1 wt.% oxygen, within the two temperature regimes: 0–200 K (dominated by quantum and impurity scattering) and 300–1200 K (dominated by phonon scattering and defect interactions).
generation.structural_mediator: Intrinsic lattice defects and oxygen impurities that modify electron scattering rates and thereby alter the electrical conductivity in a temperature-dependent manner.
generation.mechanism: At low temperatures, defect and oxygen impurity scattering induce enhanced resistive effects (potentially involving quantum interference and localization effects). At high temperatures, phonon scattering combined with the influence of defects leads to modified electron mobility. The hybrid model employs ab initio methods to capture these scattering mechanisms and refines the predictions using machine-learning calibration against experimental conductivity data, overcoming the limitations of models that assume ideal, defect-free crystals.
generation.predicted_outcome: The hybrid model is predicted to yield electrical conductivity values within an approximate 20% deviation from experimental measurements in both temperature regimes, significantly outperforming conventional analytical and ab initio approaches based on defect-free crystals that typically exhibit larger discrepancies.
generation.baseline: Conventional analytical and ab initio models based on perfect crystal assumptions, which are known to deviate by more than 20% from experimental conductivity data when applied to realistic, defective samples containing ~1 wt.% oxygen.
generation.boundary: This approach is specific to bulk, polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr with ~1 wt.% oxygen and is validated only over the temperature ranges 0–200 K and 300–1200 K. Its accuracy outside these compositional or temperature limits is not guaranteed.
generation.uncertainty: While the model is expected to achieve predictions within a 20% error margin, the exact quantitative improvement may depend on the precision of the ab initio scattering calculations and the quality and range of the experimental calibration data. Further experimental validation is required to confirm the model’s robustness for all realistic sample variations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare bulk polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr samples with confirmed ~1 wt.% oxygen content. Measure temperature-resolved electrical conductivity over the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K ranges using calibrated cryogenic and high-temperature setups. Generate conductivity prediction curves using the hybrid model and compare the predicted values at key temperatures (e.g., 100 K in the low-temperature regime and 800 K in the high-temperature regime) against the measured data.
measurements: Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity from 0 K to 200 K
Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity from 300 K to 1200 K
Key conductivity values at approximately 100 K and 800 K for focused comparison
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the electrical conductivity predicted by the hybrid model deviates by more than 20% from the experimental measurements in either temperature regime, the hypothesis that the hybrid approach improves predictive accuracy over conventional idealized models will be falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).

HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. Abstract High entropy alloys based on 3d transition metals display rich and promising magnetic characteristics for various high-technology applications. Understanding their behavior at finite temperature is, however, limited by the incomplete experimental data for single-phase alloys. Here we use first-principles alloy theory to investigate the magnetic structure of polymorphic CoCrFeMnNi in the paramagnetic state by accounting for the longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) as a function of temperature. In both face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structures, the LSFs induce sizable magnetic moments for Co, Cr and Ni. The impact of LSFs is demonstrated on the phase stability, stacking fault energy and the fcc-hcp interfacial energy. The hcp phase is energetically preferable to the fcc one at cryogenic temperatures, which results in negative stacking fault energy at these conditions. With increasing temperature, the stacking fault energy increases, suppressing the formation of stacking faults and nano-twins. Our predictions are consistent with recent experimental findings.

The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available. decision.trend: Early analytical studies on refractory high‐entropy alloys focused on ideal, defect‐free crystals to predict transport and related properties. Papers based solely on perfect lattice dynamics or standard ab initio methods could capture high‐temperature phonon scattering but were unable to address the strong effects of defects and impurities (like ~1 wt.% oxygen) evident at lower temperatures. More recent work on HfNbTaTiZr (e.g., PMC11077685) has highlighted that realistic processing (with intrinsic defects and interstitial oxygen) alters mechanical and oxidation behavior, while advances using machine‐learning–driven simulations (e.g., PMC8357793) have begun to integrate disorder effects for other properties. Nevertheless, transport property predictions across the 0–200 K (quantum/impurity‐dominated) and 300–1200 K (phonon–defect scattering) regimes remain unsatisfactorily addressed.
decision.unsolved: No current approach has reliably incorporated defect scattering and the impact of oxygen impurities into predictions of electrical conductivity for realistic, polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr. The challenge is to simultaneously capture quantum/impurity effects at low temperatures and phonon-mediated scattering at high temperatures, with clear benchmarks for accuracy against experiments.
decision.lever: Develop a hybrid methodology that couples ab initio defect scattering calculations (including oxygen interactions) with machine‐learning calibration to experimental conductivity data, explicitly training separate submodels for the 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime.
decision.why: This step directly addresses the observed gap by moving beyond idealized crystal assumptions. It builds on prior evidence from studies on HfNbTaTiZr that underscore the role of intrinsic defects and oxygen (PMC11077685) and leverages the promise of ML‐enhanced potentials (PMC8357793) to incorporate complex scattering mechanisms. Calibration to experimental benchmarks will provide explicit temperature- and sample-state limits and enable falsification by, for example, an inability to predict a held-out conductivity value within a set deviation (e.g., >20% deviation at 100 K would falsify the hypothesis).
